title: Still Ledger
user: iPhone and wearable users who need to understand when and how long they were sedentary, rather than merely see a daily step total.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker has a watch that counts steps but cannot find an iPhone app that sums daily stationary/sitting time.
A fitness-log user asks for a much more accommodating daily-calorie logging flow, reinforcing that low-friction personal measurement remains a product gap.

recurrence: Two independent fitness-log requests, including a direct 2025 request for a missing sedentary metric; the consequence is lost visibility into a behavior people are trying to change.
current_workaround: Read step rings, use generic wellness apps, or manually note desk time without a usable timeline.
incumbents_and_gap: Apple Health and Fitbit expose broad activity data, while Strong/Hevy focus on workouts. They do not make importable sedentary blocks and a simple daily change target the central artifact.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA that imports Apple Health export XML or accepts quick manual intervals, shows a private day/week sedentary timeline, and lets a user set a realistic interruption target. Non-goals: health diagnosis, live sensor collection, coaching, or social feeds.
success_measure: In a 21-day pilot, 50% of active users import or log 14+ days and report at least three days with fewer sedentary blocks than their first-week baseline.
monetization: one-time — a local personal metric should not require an ongoing subscription.
constraints: Process exports in-browser; do not upload health data; make health-export parsing resilient to large/untrusted XML; present correlations only, never medical claims.
why_distinct: This is a focused sedentary-time ledger and reflection loop, not another wearable dashboard or generalized wellness app.

title: Set Receipt
user: Regular lifters who want to record a set as quickly as writing “225x5” in a notebook and retain a compact proof of the workout.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A lifter who tried 15+ apps returns to a notebook because logging one set takes too many taps and asks for an actually fast, minimal alternative.
The open fitness tracker has a multi-comment request for syncing data with other trackers, showing that preserving and moving a training record matters to users.

recurrence: One direct 2026 account names repeated abandonment after many apps; a separate fitness-tool discussion has 13 comments around data synchronization. Friction happens every set, so severity is high for adherent users.
current_workaround: Paper notebooks, Notes, spreadsheets, or feature-heavy trackers with paywalls and feeds.
incumbents_and_gap: Strong, Hevy, and Jefit provide deep programs and social/product upsell surfaces; their primary interaction is not a one-line, keyboard-first set entry with a portable workout receipt.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with a text grammar for sets (for example, 225x5), editable exercise aliases, rest timer, and a shareable/printable receipt containing volume, duration, and PRs. Non-goals: exercise video library, meal plans, social challenges, or AI coaching.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot lifters log 12 workouts in 30 days with median set-entry time below five seconds.
monetization: one-time — core logging has clear personal utility but no running-service cost.
constraints: Keep data local and exportable as CSV/JSON; make accessibility and large tap targets work in gyms; do not give training or injury advice.
why_distinct: The product is an ultra-fast immutable workout receipt, not a broad fitness platform.

title: Dose Witness
user: Families coordinating an elderly relative’s medications who need every caregiver to see whether a particular dose was actually given.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An asker says an elderly relative loses track of many medications; a shared Google Doc is not kept current, and they explicitly seek a non-data-mining dedicated app.
A household medication integration was created because calendar/to-do reminders do not record whether a dose was given, re-nag, or sync the done state among caregivers.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 household-care accounts identify the same failure: reminders exist but accountable shared completion does not. Missed or duplicate doses make severity high.
current_workaround: Shared documents, calendar alarms, text messages, and verbal handoffs.
incumbents_and_gap: Medisafe, Apple Reminders, and generic shared task apps remind individuals; they either require accounts/data sharing or do not give a simple household-visible dose witness and exception handoff.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first PWA for one household: medication cards, scheduled doses, an explicit given/skipped/uncertain status, caregiver initials, offline printable handoff, and encrypted export/import between devices. Non-goals: interaction checking, prescription changes, pharmacy ordering, or clinical advice.
success_measure: A five-household pilot records 95% of scheduled doses with a status for 30 consecutive days and resolves a missed/uncertain dose without phone-tag in at least three cases.
monetization: one-time — privacy-sensitive family coordination is a poor fit for an advertising or data-mining model.
constraints: Clear “not a medical device” positioning; encryption for exported records; no dosage recommendations; accessible type, contrast, and large controls for older adults.
why_distinct: It records shared responsibility for an actual dose, not just a medication list or an alarm.

title: StepDown Card
user: People following a clinician-provided medication taper who need a clear, private day-by-day regimen they can acknowledge and export.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Dosis is presented as a private, on-device medication tracker, indicating current demand for medication tracking outside account/data-collection models.
The open-source MedTimer project has an explicit request for automatic taper scheduling.

recurrence: Independent 2026 privacy-first tracking and taper-scheduling requests show a narrow but consequential workflow not covered by a standard daily reminder.
current_workaround: Calendar events, annotated pill bottles, handwritten date tables, or manually altering repeating reminders.
incumbents_and_gap: Medisafe and MedTimer handle reminders and stock; a clinician-authored finite schedule with visible dose steps, acknowledgement, and a printable handoff is often awkward or hidden.
smallest_useful_product: A local offline scheduler where the user enters a clinician’s exact start date, dose steps, and end date; it produces a calendar card, acknowledgement log, and printable summary. Non-goals: calculating taper plans, recommending dosage, drug-interaction checks, or notifications that claim clinical reliability.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot users can enter a supplied taper schedule without help and export a correct schedule card in under five minutes.
monetization: one-time — the app holds sensitive, episodic personal data and has no required hosted service.
constraints: Require the user to enter clinician instructions verbatim; show prominent safety language; local encryption option and no network dependency; no medical-device claims.
why_distinct: It is a faithful schedule-transcription and acknowledgement tool, not an AI health advisor or generalized pill reminder.

title: Recipe Exit Pack
user: People leaving a single-platform recipe app who need their own recipes, notes, photos, and source attribution in a portable offline format.

evidence.quote_or_summary: CookPal’s current pitch is importing recipes from websites, TikTok, and YouTube into clean cards, illustrating how recipe collections become tied to capture tools and varied sources.
A Mela user moving beyond Apple devices built a converter to portable Markdown and still had to manually convert HEIC images after import.

recurrence: Two 2026 sources show recipe capture is active while platform migration and media portability remain manual. The pain is acute when a household changes devices or an app’s terms/pricing.
current_workaround: Manual copy/paste, screenshots, app-specific exports, and one-off command-line scripts.
incumbents_and_gap: Paprika, Mela, CookPal, and Mealie organize recipes, but portability across ecosystems often loses images, source links, tags, and user notes or demands technical conversion.
smallest_useful_product: A browser-local importer for user-exported recipe files and pasted recipe text that writes a zip of human-readable Markdown, normalized images, JSON metadata, and a source/attribution manifest. Non-goals: scraping paywalled sites, mass web crawling, social-media downloading, or recipe recommendations.
success_measure: At least 90% of a 100-recipe test export preserves title, ingredients, steps, notes, and a viewable image; 70% of testers open the resulting archive in a second app without support.
monetization: one-time — conversion is occasional and should run locally rather than turn personal collections into a hosted data product.
constraints: Only transform user-supplied exports/content; preserve source URL and attribution; do all conversion in-browser; do not bypass access controls or redistribute copyrighted recipe media.
why_distinct: It is an exit and preservation utility, not another recipe subscription, scraper, or AI recipe generator.

title: Dinner Binder
user: Households with digital recipe collections who need a clean, reliable printable cooking packet for a week, trip, or screen-free kitchen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A recipe manager pitches cross-device organization and automatic nutrition information, showing the current concentration of recipe value inside digital apps.
A 20-reaction, 20-comment Mealie request calls for exporting individual recipes and full cookbooks to standard printable PDF.

recurrence: A current recipe-management launch and a high-engagement open-source request both point to the persistent handoff from digital collections to a usable cooking artifact.
current_workaround: Print browser pages with ads/layout noise, take screenshots, or manually format a document before a trip or meal plan.
incumbents_and_gap: Mealie, Paprika, and Tandoor manage broad recipe libraries; their print/export features are secondary, often need a server, and rarely make a selected meal run with consolidated prep central.
smallest_useful_product: A static offline web app that accepts Markdown/JSON recipe files, selects recipes and servings, creates a paginated print packet with ingredient checkboxes, consolidated prep timeline, and optional allergen notes. Non-goals: web recipe import, nutrition calculation, shopping delivery, or hosted accounts.
success_measure: In testing, 80% of users can turn three supplied recipes into a correctly paginated, readable print packet in under three minutes.
monetization: one-time — printing and formatting need no ongoing infrastructure.
constraints: Input only user-owned/exported recipes; preserve attribution fields; support printer-safe CSS and accessible typography; no dietary or allergy safety guarantees.
why_distinct: The output is a dependable, selected cooking run—not a recipe database with a print button bolted on.

title: Pantry Check
user: Busy shared households that want to stop duplicate purchases and expiry waste without performing full inventory updates after every meal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The iPantry maker describes duplicate purchases and forgotten expired food in a shared household; existing apps were too complex or account-locked.
A 13-reaction, 15-comment feature request asks for a recorded inventory-reconcile workflow that confirms stock even when the count has not changed and surfaces items by last check date.

recurrence: The 2025 household complaint and high-engagement inventory feature request identify the same issue: inventory decays unless checking it is deliberately lightweight.
current_workaround: Mental lists, generic grocery lists, occasional spreadsheet stocktakes, or full pantry applications that go stale.
incumbents_and_gap: Grocy, Pantry Check, and kitchen inventory apps support detailed stock records; the gap is a quick confidence-based reconciliation session instead of requiring exact transaction tracking for every item.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with zones (fridge/freezer/pantry), quick “seen/used/expired” swipes, last-confirmed age, low-confidence queue, and a shareable shopping delta. Non-goals: barcode catalog dependence, grocery ordering, receipt OCR, or nutrition tracking.
success_measure: At least half of pilot households complete four weekly reconciliation sessions and reduce self-reported duplicate purchases by 25% over six weeks.
monetization: one-time — shared household stock should work without an account or per-seat service.
constraints: Local data with explicit encrypted export for sharing; no retailer integrations; expiry prompts must be advisory, not food-safety guarantees.
why_distinct: It manages uncertainty through short reconcile passes rather than pretending households will maintain a perfect inventory ledger.

title: Bed Seasons
user: Hobby gardeners who need a visual bed plan that also remembers perennials and adapts a planting checklist to their own frost dates.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A UK gardener built a climate-aware planner after generic apps suggested tomato timing that did not fit local conditions; they report ongoing permanent-plant tracking is what users pay for.
A gardener explicitly asks for a free Mac/web visual planner, ideally able to lay out beds and plants from a photographed plan.

recurrence: The newer climate-aware planner and an independent visual-layout request describe complementary recurring jobs: what is planted where, and what is timely here. Seasonal use makes missed timing costly for a whole year.
current_workaround: Paper sketches, generic USDA-zone calendars, spreadsheets, or a one-time garden-planner mockup that does not carry forward plant history.
incumbents_and_gap: Seedtime, GrowVeg, and Leaftide offer broader planning, subscriptions, or hosted accounts. A compact local bed history plus user-entered frost-date schedule remains a smaller privacy-first wedge.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with drag-and-drop rectangular beds, perennial/annual history, user-entered last/first frost dates, and a generated sow/transplant/maintenance checklist. Non-goals: plant disease diagnosis, weather prediction, seed marketplace, or automated image recognition.
success_measure: At least 60% of spring pilot users recreate two beds and return to mark three seasonal tasks within 45 days.
monetization: one-time — gardens are seasonal and a local plan has negligible operating cost.
constraints: Make climate assumptions transparent and editable; no guarantee of crop success; all garden/location data stays on device; use only openly licensed/default crop guidance.
why_distinct: It combines a durable bed memory with a deliberately simple local schedule, instead of an AI plant adviser or generic calendar.

title: Weekboard
user: Cross-platform families who need a simple shared weekly view without committing their household schedule to Google, Apple, or a new subscription account.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent asks for a simple self-hostable family calendar that works on Android and Apple, specifically tired of evaluating too many projects.
A nearly Google-free household needs shared calendars across people, operating systems, and devices, with migration from Google but without unsuitable bundle pricing.

recurrence: Two 2025 cross-platform/privacy requests show the problem is choosing and maintaining a simple family view, not a lack of full enterprise calendar systems.
current_workaround: Google Calendar, Apple Family Sharing, paper calendars, or testing/self-hosting several CalDAV products.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, Nextcloud, and Radicale solve calendar storage; none offers a tiny, household-first weekly board with no account and a clean local export/import handoff as its whole product.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA weekly board with people/lane colors, recurring events, printable view, and standard ICS import/export; sharing is an explicit encrypted file/QR handoff. Non-goals: email invitations, cloud sync, chat, contacts, or a CalDAV server.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 70% of households publish or exchange an updated ICS board weekly and report fewer than one missed shared commitment per household per month.
monetization: one-time — no-account local operation keeps the scope and cost aligned with the privacy request.
constraints: Use standard ICS without silently sending event data; document that file/QR exchange is not real-time sync; handle timezone and recurrence rules carefully.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately constrained family-facing calendar surface, not another hosted calendar provider.

title: Done Here
user: Households that need recurring chores to have a visible completion history and a compact calendar record, not just an overdue task badge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A household released an open-source, no-account family calendar, demonstrating active demand for shared household coordination without account creation.
Grocy’s chores-analysis request has 12 comments and asks for per-chore execution histories, cadence, and a fair view of who completed work.

recurrence: A current no-account household-calendar launch plus a long-commented chores-analysis request show that schedules alone do not answer whether a recurring job happened.
current_workaround: Repeating reminders, whiteboards, shared task apps, arguments over memory, and checking off tasks without retaining meaningful history.
incumbents_and_gap: Tody, Sweepy, and Grocy track chores; they emphasize gamification, scores, or broad household ERP. The unresolved small artifact is a trustworthy completed-event calendar with evidence/note and cadence at a glance.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with named recurring chores, a one-tap completion event, optional photo/note, last-done and next-due display, and ICS/PDF history export. Non-goals: points economies, child surveillance, chat, payroll-style fairness scoring, or cloud accounts.
success_measure: Pilot households record 80% of configured recurring chores for four weeks and can answer when each of their top five chores was last completed without asking another person.
monetization: one-time — accountability data should remain local and the utility needs no hosted service.
constraints: Local-only by default; consent-aware photo handling; no rankings that encourage coercive household monitoring; ICS export must use valid timezone-aware timestamps.
why_distinct: The core output is a calm proof-of-completion timeline, not task gamification or an all-purpose family platform.

title: House Receipt
user: Homeowners who need a durable, shareable history of maintenance work, warranties, costs, and photos when a repair recurs or a contractor asks what happened before.

evidence.quote_or_summary: HouseTrak was built because home information was scattered across notes, photos, emails, spreadsheets, and reminders whenever something broke or needed maintenance.
A user with many home-maintenance tasks asks to log completed work to a calendar, rather than leave completion buried in a task manager.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–2026 accounts identify fragmentation after work is completed; the pain resurfaces during expensive repeat repairs, handoffs, and sales.
current_workaround: Notes, email receipts, photos, task-manager completions, spreadsheets, and paper folders.
incumbents_and_gap: Centriq, HomeZada, and HouseTrak aim to become all-in-one home apps. Their breadth creates setup burden; a local service receipt that turns one completed job into a durable record is a narrower need.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with a single job receipt: component/location, completion date, cost, contractor, warranty expiry, photos, and next service date; export as a PDF or encrypted archive. Non-goals: contractor marketplace, repair diagnosis, insurance claims, or smart-home integration.
success_measure: In a 60-day pilot, 60% of users create five service receipts and can retrieve a prior job’s date, cost, and warranty in under 30 seconds.
monetization: one-time — local records and PDF exports do not require a recurring service.
constraints: Photos and contractor information remain on-device; make backups/export obvious; avoid legal or insurance coverage claims; support common document-size limits in export.
why_distinct: It makes a completed maintenance job a portable evidence packet instead of becoming another sprawling home-management database.

title: Today Money
user: People who budget manually and do not want bank sync, but need a trustworthy answer to what can be spent today after upcoming obligations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A long-time YNAB user built an alternative after finding $109/year unjustifiable when they never used bank sync.
Actual Budget’s balance-forecast feedback issue has 20 comments, showing continued demand for projecting cash after scheduled commitments.

recurrence: Two 2026 budgeting communities independently surface the same need: users want useful planning and forecasts without paying for or surrendering data to bank-sync services.
current_workaround: YNAB/Actual, Google Sheets, mentally subtracting bills, or downloading transactions into a larger finance package.
incumbents_and_gap: YNAB, Actual, Monarch, and Copilot cover full budgeting. The gap is a local, deliberately tiny daily-safe-to-spend view built from manual balances and committed bills rather than a complete financial system.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA where a user enters current cash, mandatory future bills, and protected envelopes; it computes a conservative daily amount through the next payday and exposes assumptions. Non-goals: bank connections, investment tracking, credit scoring, tax advice, or shared cloud accounts.
success_measure: At least 70% of 30-day pilot users update the balance weekly and correctly predict whether a planned discretionary purchase fits their protected-bills plan in a follow-up check.
monetization: one-time — manual local budgeting avoids ongoing aggregation costs and aligns with the anti-subscription evidence.
constraints: No financial advice or bank credential collection; calculations must be transparent and exportable; data stays on-device with optional encrypted backup; support multi-currency only after the single-currency core works.
why_distinct: It answers one high-frequency decision conservatively, rather than cloning a full envelope-budget suite or wrapping an LLM around transactions.
